question: Which of the following correctly states the standard surgical timetable for repair of cleft lip and palate?

answers.text: Lip repair at 3 months; palate repair at 9–12 months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The lip is repaired at approximately 3 months (rule of tens: weight ≥10 lb, Hb ≥10 g/dL, age ≥10 weeks) to restore feeding and appearance early. The palate is repaired between 9 and 12 months — before meaningful speech development — to allow normal velopharyngeal function.

answers.text: Both lip and palate repaired together in a single operation at 6 months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A combined single-stage repair is not standard practice. Lip repair is performed earlier (~3 months) to optimise function and parent–infant bonding; palate repair is staged later (9–12 months) to coincide with pre-speech development.

answers.text: Palate repair first at 3 months, followed by lip repair at 12 months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The sequence is the reverse of standard practice. The lip is repaired first (~3 months) to restore anatomy and feeding; the palate is repaired later (9–12 months) before speech development.

answers.text: Both repairs are deferred until after the permanent dentition erupts at age 6–7 years

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This timing is far too late. Early lip repair improves feeding and appearance; early palate repair is critical for normal speech. Deferring to school age would cause severe developmental consequences.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: Lip repair ~3 months (before 6 months, after weight/Hb thresholds met). Palate repair 9–12 months (before the child starts to develop speech). The purpose of each stage drives its timing.
Correct. Lip at ~3 months (rule of tens), palate at 9–12 months before speech. The timetable is driven by functional milestones, not arbitrary ages.
